summary: The note covers Milltown's September 15, 2023 municipal election, the first held under Ranked Choice Voting (RCV), adopted by the city council on the recommendation of a committee led by Dr. Julia Enderby. It describes how RCV increased the number of candidates, changed campaign rhetoric, raised voter turnout to 65%, and produced a four-round count won by Liz Montgomery. It also discusses implementation costs, the role of media, and expectations for more collaborative governance and wider reform.
one_line: Milltown's 2023 first use of Ranked Choice Voting boosted candidates and turnout, shifted campaigns toward consensus, and raised questions about cost and governance.
key_facts: Milltown held a municipal election on September 15, 2023, its first using Ranked Choice Voting (RCV), to elect a new mayor and council members.
The city council approved RCV about eight months before the election, following a recommendation from a committee led by political scientist Dr. Julia Enderby.
RCV lets voters rank candidates in order of preference and is designed to ensure officials win with a majority rather than a plurality.
Milltown's mayoral races had previously fielded no more than five candidates; this year twelve ran.
Jane Hall, a local bakery owner and first-time candidate, said RCV meant she did not have to be the 'lesser of two evils'.
Mayoral hopeful Michael Chen said on October 3 that candidates must be 'a consensus candidate' and focus on community issues rather than partisan divisions.
Preliminary figures released October 5 showed 65% of eligible voters cast a ballot, compared with 48% in the previous election.
Counting took place on October 20 and required four rounds because no candidate had a majority on the first count.
Liz Montgomery, a former school principal, won the mayoral race after redistribution of votes from eliminated candidates.
Council member Tom Baines, elected alongside Montgomery, said on October 25 that the council could become 'a model of cooperative governance'.
Implementing RCV required spending on voter education, new voting equipment and poll worker training, which some critics said would divert funds from essential services.
Financial analyst Jennifer Clark argues RCV yields long-term savings by avoiding expensive run-off elections.
The Milltown Gazette held information sessions and published explainers on how RCV works.
Discussions have begun about applying RCV principles to other levels of government.
